draft.title: The fall of Singapore
card: Singapore was a British naval base and fortress in South-East Asia. Many Australians believed it protected Australia from attack by Japan.
Japan invaded Malaya in December 1941 and moved down towards Singapore. On 15 February 1942, the British forces in Singapore surrendered.
About 15,000 Australian soldiers were captured and became prisoners of war (POWs). Many of them were held in harsh conditions by the Japanese.
The fall was a shock to Australians. It showed that Britain could not defend Australia, and Australia began to look for other protection.
draft.remember: Singapore fell in February 1942, and Australians saw that Britain could not protect them.

a.q: Why did the fall of Singapore shock many Australians?
opts: It showed that Britain could not defend Australia
It showed that Japan had no plans to attack Australia
It ended Australia's involvement in the Pacific War
It proved that Australia no longer needed an army
a.why: Many Australians had relied on Singapore and Britain for protection. When the fortress fell, it showed that Britain could not defend Australia. It did not end the war, because Australia kept fighting.
a.clue: Think about what Singapore was believed to protect.

b.q: In March 1942, Tom reads in a Sydney paper that Singapore has fallen and that thousands of Australians are prisoners of war. What would he most likely conclude about Australia's safety?
opts: Britain may not be able to protect Australia from Japan
Japan has been defeated and Australia is now safe
Australia should leave the war and make peace with Japan
Australia's army is no longer needed in the Pacific
b.why: The fall of Singapore broke the belief that Britain's fortress would shield Australia. Tom would see that Australia was exposed to Japan. The idea that Japan was defeated is wrong, because Japan had just won a major victory.
b.clue: Remember what Singapore was thought to guard against.

a.best: It showed that Britain could not defend Australia

b.best: Britain may not be able to protect Australia from Japan

problems.detail: The right option is the only one with a hedge ('may not be able'), while every distractor is an absolute claim. A student could pick it on that cue alone, without knowing the idea.

problems.detail: 'the British forces in Singapore surrendered' could suggest only British troops surrendered, which sits oddly with the next line about 15,000 Australians being captured. The surrendering force was British-led but included Australian, Indian and other Commonwealth troops; 'the British-led forces, including Australians,' would be clearer.
